entry.title: How Forge Structures Requests for Prompt Cache Reuse
entry.summary:

entry.content:
I am building Forge, an open-source coding environment that brings agent conversations, editing, repository navigation, a terminal, and Git into one workspace.

An early problem was cost. The OpenCode Go weekly allowance would barely last a day of coding. On a self-funded project, that was difficult to sustain.

Coding requests repeatedly send instructions and conversation history. If the provider can reuse a cached prefix, that repeated input can cost less. The harness cannot decide what the provider caches, but it can avoid changing content unnecessarily.

This article explains how Forge constructs requests for that reuse and presents the results of a controlled evaluation. The reported cache-hit ratios are results for those workloads, not a guarantee for every coding session.

Why Prompt Caching

Coding requests often repeat instructions and context from earlier requests. Reprocessing the shared context consumes avoidable costs and time. During inference, a model processes the input and creates intermediate key-value (KV) states, and then generates one token at a time. With prompt caching, a provider can retain eligible KV states for the prompt prefix, and later reuse them if a new request starts with the same prefix. Cache eligibility and reuse depend on the provider's caching strategy. A coding harness can improve the chance of reuse by ordering request content so that stable instructions and context come before content that changes between requests.

We set an internal target of 95% cache-hit ratio. Comparisons with other harnesses require comparable workloads, providers, and measurement methods; a single aggregate number would not tell us whether our request construction was working.

How Forge Constructs Requests

Forge puts stable content first and new content last. Changing an early instruction can invalidate reuse for everything after it.

Forge's request path has two layers.

  • A canonical request: Forge's provider-neutral ModelRequest object.
  • A wire request: a provider adapter serializes ModelRequest for the selected API.

To build the canonical request, Forge:

  • Starts by creating the system message: It contains system prompt, workspace's AGENTS.md, and discovered Skills. Before being added to the system message, Skills are sorted by name, and the session's scratch directory is inserted in the system prompt.
  • Keeps the system message in conversation history. On resumption of a prior session, Forge replays the journal, and uses the stored system message. This ensures that the cache is not invalidated on the resumption of an old session with a different system message.
  • Appends the user message, assistant replies and tool results to the end of the message.
  • Before each model step, it repairs and compacts the history, if required. Compaction rewrites the context, and starts a new cache epoch, because the old prefix no longer describes the prompt.
  • Finally creates a ModelRequest. This bundles the transcript, selected tools and model, workspace root, route and session IDs, reasoning settings, and prompt_cache: true.

The provider adapter then constructs the wire request.

  • Anthropic: It places cache markers at useful boundaries. Forge marks the last system block, the last tool definition, and current conversation tail. As the conversation grows, the conversation marker moves to the new tail; the system and tool markers remain at their ends.
  • OpenAI-compatible APIs: It sends the conversation as messages containing system, user, assistant replies and tools in order. Forge converts each tool into function schemas, and adds a workspace-derived prompt_cache_key

How Forge Keeps the Prefix Stable

To keep the prefix stable, Forge implements:

  • Intact prior history: New user turns and tool results extend the transcript, preserving earlier messages.
  • Sorted variable lists: Tool names and Skills are sorted to prevent incidental map or filesystem order from changing the prompt.
  • Frozen content: Image snapshots and frozen tool outputs prevent later file changes from altering old transcript entries.
  • Preserved system instructions: The journaled system message is kept rather than regenerated from whatever instructions happen to exist now.
  • Cache routing: Forge hashes the workspace path into prompt_cache_key, which helps the provider caching algorithm with routing affinity across all the sessions of the same workspace.

How We Measured Cache Hits

For each model response, Forge reads the provider-reported cached-input token count and normalises it.

  • Anthropic: Reports cache_read_input_tokens
  • OpenAI-compatible APIs: Provides cached_tokens in token-details fields.

Forge adds the cached and uncached input tokens across the model calls. It normalises total prompt tokens across providers, since Anthropic reports uncached input separately while OpenAI includes cached tokens in its total.

How We Evaluated Prompt Caching

We tested Forge's cache-aware request flow, with the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, OpenCode Go subscription. The evaluation used snapshot of tool calls, repository content and system instructions. We used three different use cases to cover different scenarios.

  1. The conversation grows: We start with the same system message. Each following request adds the same user message, assistant reply, and tool result. This measures cache reuse as the conversation gets longer.
  2. Only the ending changes: We keep the beginning of each request identical and change only the final user message or tool result. This measures whether Forge can reuse the earlier part when recent context changes.
  3. An early instruction change: We change one line in the workspace instructions, then send the same later conversation and tool results. This measures where reuse stops when an early part of the prompt changes. We then repeat the changed request to measure reuse of the new prefix.

For each use case we ran the evaluation 10 times.

Results and Findings

The mean, minimum, maximum, and standard deviation are calculated across 10 cache-aware runs per use case. The token-weighted ratio is calculated as total cache-read tokens divided by total input tokens.

Use case Runs Mean hit ratio Min Max Standard Deviation Token-weighted hit ratio
Conversation grows 10 99.60% 99.30% 99.90% 0.19 pp 99.60%
Only the ending changes 10 99.48% 99.10% 99.86% 0.24 pp 99.48%
An early instruction changes 10 94.80% 93.20% 96.40% 1.04 pp 94.80%

Token totals are summed across the 10 runs for each case. Uncached input is the remainder after cache reads and cache writes are subtracted from total input.

Use case Total input tokens Cache-read tokens Cache-write tokens Uncached input tokens
Conversation grows 1,284,763 1,279,623 2,743 2,397
Only the ending changes 1,115,482 1,109,682 3,271 2,529
An early instruction changes 963,247 913,159 17,633 32,455
  • Appending messages or changing only the last message resulted in improved cache-hit ratios, as reflected by 99.60% and 99.48% mean cache-hit ratios for the first two use cases.
  • Changing the instruction, which is in the early part of the message, drops the cache-hit ratio by about 5 percentage points compared to the other use cases, and leaves about 32,000 uncached input tokens, compared with about 2,500 in each of the first two cases.
  • The early change use case varies more (~1 pp standard deviation) between runs compared to the other use cases (~0.2-0.25 pp standard deviation), indicating caching is more sensitive to the early message changes.

What this establishes

Prompt caching is a request-design problem shared by the harness and provider. The harness controls request ordering, history persistence, and cache hints; the provider determines which prefixes it retains and reuses. Tracking usage alongside serialized request snapshots connects cache behavior to the prefix that produced it. These results describe controlled request sequences on one provider/model route. They do not establish the same hit ratio across providers or ordinary interactive sessions. Cache expiry, concurrency, changing tools, and compaction can all affect reuse.

Design request construction and cache observability together. Otherwise you can preserve the prefix carefully and still have no way to tell whether the provider reused it.

entry.title: What engineering managers need to own as AI changes delivery
entry.summary:
I think engineering management built mainly around status tracking is becoming harder to justify.

That is narrower than saying managers are disappearing. Someone still has to set priorities, develop people, resolve disagreements, and take responsibility when a technically successful project produces little business value.

AI-assisted development changes some of that …
entry.content:
I think engineering management built mainly around status tracking is becoming harder to justify.

That is narrower than saying managers are disappearing. Someone still has to set priorities, develop people, resolve disagreements, and take responsibility when a technically successful project produces little business value.

AI-assisted development changes some of that work. It does not tell us how many engineers one manager can responsibly support.

More output creates different constraints

Agents can reduce the effort of some implementation tasks. The benefit depends on the work, the tools, and how much verification it needs.

When implementation becomes faster, selecting the right work and evaluating the result matter more. Producing another service is not useful if nobody needs it or the team cannot operate it.

I expect leaders who understand those constraints to remain valuable. A manager whose main contribution is collecting updates has a weaker case.

That is an interpretation of where the work is going, not a reliable forecast of an org chart.

People management is real work

It is easy to dismiss one-on-ones as meetings until an engineer needs feedback, a conflict is blocking delivery, or someone is being quietly overloaded.

Automation may improve coordination. It does not make trust, coaching, or fair evaluation free. Increasing spans of control without reducing that burden can simply leave people with less support.

A flatter organisation can make decisions faster. It can also concentrate authority and leave ambiguity unresolved for longer. Fewer layers is not automatically a better design.

The kind of leadership I would invest in

I would keep enough technical depth to challenge designs, inspect agent-generated work, and understand operational risks. That does not require being the best programmer in the team. It does require more than following a dashboard.

I would also learn how the company makes money, which customers shape the roadmap, and where engineering effort changes the outcome. Technical quality matters, but it needs a connection to something the business is trying to achieve.

Finally, I would examine the system around the team: incentives, dependencies, ownership, and how decisions get made. Some delivery problems cannot be fixed inside a sprint.

What remains uncertain

One company's management ratio would not establish what works across engineering organisations. Staffing targets tell us what a company intends to change, not whether that change improves delivery or support.

AI may change the balance between implementation, review, and coordination. Team maturity, product risk, and organisational complexity will still matter.

My position is simpler: technical judgment, business understanding, and people leadership are worth developing together. A title will not do that work for you.

entry.title: Near-real-time is a product promise, not a Kafka cluster
entry.summary:
Before building a streaming pipeline, I want to know which decision improves when the data arrives sooner.

“Near-real-time” can mean seconds to one team and an updated dashboard before a morning meeting to another. Neither meaning tells you to buy a Kafka cluster.

On LinkedIn's Enterprise Data Platform (EDP), BI …
entry.content:
Before building a streaming pipeline, I want to know which decision improves when the data arrives sooner.

“Near-real-time” can mean seconds to one team and an updated dashboard before a morning meeting to another. Neither meaning tells you to buy a Kafka cluster.

On LinkedIn's Enterprise Data Platform (EDP), BI consumers already had working batch paths. The useful discussion was about trustworthy data in their actual workflows, and what it would take to migrate them.

Put a bound on usable data

Name the dataset, consumer, and maximum acceptable age at the point of use. Define the normal operating conditions and what happens when the bound is missed.

“Usable” matters. An event arriving at ingestion is not the same as a validated record available in a dashboard. BI extracts and caches can erase the benefit of a fast upstream pipeline.

Measure source-to-consumer delay before choosing the architecture. If an hourly extract dominates it, shaving milliseconds off processing will not deliver the promised experience.

Check whether faster is worth the cost

A weekly reporting workflow may be well served by a reliable batch delivery. A decision that becomes invalid after minutes needs a different design.

The cost is broader than infrastructure. Streaming introduces ordering, replay, late events, state, and recovery work. You need operators who can explain what consumers see during catch-up, not just while the pipeline is healthy.

Choose the bound first. Then work out the least complicated system that can keep it.

Migration is part of delivery

For BI teams using Power BI and Tableau, moving to EDP meant taking on migration effort and performance risk. Their existing path still produced data. Resistance was understandable.

EDP engineers helped with migration. Connectors reduced integration work. Performance after cutover became our responsibility. Deprecation milestones gave dual running an end.

Those choices made adoption practical. Faster infrastructure alone would not have done it.

Define disagreement and failure

During cutover, which source wins if old and new numbers differ? Who can pause a bad publish? How do consumers know the data is late or incomplete?

A migration milestone is not a freshness SLO. Once the consumer is on the new path, measure the continuing time and correctness promise separately.

I would start with high-value datasets, prove the path with named consumers, and expand from there. A platform does not need to stream everything to be useful.

The achievement is a better decision made in time. A busy event log is supporting evidence at best.

entry.title: The platform team’s real job is interfaces
entry.summary:
A platform can be strategically important and still be irrelevant to the team asked to adopt it.

At LinkedIn, the Enterprise Data Platform (EDP) was intended to be the governed path for go-to-market datasets. BI teams using Power BI and Tableau already had Hadoop-based pipelines. Those pipelines worked well enough …
entry.content:
A platform can be strategically important and still be irrelevant to the team asked to adopt it.

At LinkedIn, the Enterprise Data Platform (EDP) was intended to be the governed path for go-to-market datasets. BI teams using Power BI and Tableau already had Hadoop-based pipelines. Those pipelines worked well enough for their current needs.

From their perspective, migration was more work with a chance of making dashboards slower. We had to solve that problem before our platform strategy could mean anything.

The API was only part of the interface

The practical interface included getting a dataset into a BI workflow, understanding its meaning, obtaining access, migrating an existing workbook, and finding help when something failed.

Storage and processing choices mattered internally. Consumers needed a predictable way to finish their work.

This is where platform teams can misread adoption. A team declining a migration may be responding sensibly to its delivery commitments. Asking it to absorb your platform's cost does not make the cost disappear.

Fund the transition

We worked with leadership to make adoption a priority and legacy deprecation an explicit continuity concern.

Then EDP engineers took on migration work: connectors, pairing, tooling, and query performance. Office hours gave partners a regular place to resolve blockers.

The sponsorship and the capacity were both necessary. A mandate without support would have transferred the problem to BI. Support without prioritisation would have left it competing indefinitely with their existing roadmap.

Finish the migration

Our definition of done included moving the scoped GTM paths onto EDP and decommissioning redundant pipelines. The concentrated BI effort took roughly a quarter.

Dual running was useful while validating the new path. Leaving both sources alive indefinitely would have preserved the ambiguity we were trying to remove.

Deprecation needs dates, owners, and exit criteria. Extensions sometimes make sense. Each one should have a reason and a revised plan, rather than becoming a quiet default.

Own the experience after adoption

If a dashboard becomes slower after cutover, the platform team cannot declare success because the connector works. Adoption is a promise about the workflow, including support and performance.

I would judge a platform by whether consumers can succeed on it, whether their costs are visible, and whether the old paths can actually end.

Infrastructure provides the capability. The interface determines whether anyone can use it.

entry.title: When I still choose a relational database
entry.summary:
In 2013, I wrote RDBMS vs. NOSQL? because database advice was getting ahead of database requirements.

I still start with a relational database for many product backends. Users, accounts, permissions, orders, and configuration usually have relationships and invariants that fit the model well.

That is a default, not a loyalty …
entry.content:
In 2013, I wrote RDBMS vs. NOSQL? because database advice was getting ahead of database requirements.

I still start with a relational database for many product backends. Users, accounts, permissions, orders, and configuration usually have relationships and invariants that fit the model well.

That is a default, not a loyalty programme. A different workload can justify a different store.

Start with the things that must stay correct

If the product needs several records to change together, transactions can make correctness much easier to reason about. Moving that responsibility into application code is a choice with an ongoing cost.

I also value the ability to evolve queries. Early products change their questions. A relational schema with appropriate indexes often accommodates that more easily than a store built around a narrow access pattern.

Operational familiarity matters. A team that knows how to diagnose, restore, and run a database has an advantage over a team operating its theoretically ideal store for the first time.

None of this excuses ignoring load. Measure the workload and test the recovery path.

Move specialised work out when it earns its place

The primary database does not need to answer every question.

Search, analytics, high-volume telemetry, and some graph or time-series workloads may benefit from separate systems. Treat those as deliberate read models or specialist stores, with a clear source of truth and a way to rebuild them.

Before moving the transactional core, I want evidence of the limit: write saturation, state size, contention, unacceptable recovery time, or a topology requirement the current system cannot meet.

Read replicas help read capacity. They do not remove every write or consistency constraint. A bigger machine is also a plan with a limit, not an insult to distributed systems.

The seams become your responsibility

Once data moves between stores, you need change propagation, replay, failure handling, and a definition of acceptable lag.

Avoid casual dual writes. If one write succeeds and the other fails, somebody must know how to detect and repair the difference. Derived systems simplify the primary workload only if their recovery is designed.

The same reasoning applies to service boundaries. Keep capabilities together where shared invariants dominate. Split them where independent operation or deployment pays for the additional coordination.

Ask before adding a primary store

  1. Which queries and invariants does the product need?
  2. What data volume and throughput do we expect, with headroom?
  3. Where will multi-record correctness be enforced?
  4. How will access patterns and schemas change?
  5. Who will operate it and restore it after failure?
  6. Which measured requirement rules out the simpler option?

NoSQL covers many different systems and trade-offs. It is not a single alternative to SQL, much less a sign that the architecture has become serious.

Use the system that fits the work. Prefer the one your team can explain and recover.

entry.title: Freshness SLOs: the metric product teams actually feel
entry.summary:
A pipeline can be green while the dashboard is wrong. Or late. Or showing a different number from the other dashboard everyone also calls official.

At LinkedIn, the Enterprise Data Platform (EDP) was intended to become the governed source for go-to-market data. BI teams could already get data through Hadoop-based …
entry.content:
A pipeline can be green while the dashboard is wrong. Or late. Or showing a different number from the other dashboard everyone also calls official.

At LinkedIn, the Enterprise Data Platform (EDP) was intended to become the governed source for go-to-market data. BI teams could already get data through Hadoop-based pipelines. Moving them onto EDP meant dealing with the entire path to a usable dashboard, including the parts outside our platform.

That is why I care about freshness separately from request latency.

A fast query can return old data

Latency measures how long a request takes. Freshness measures how old the data is when someone uses it.

An API can respond in 100 milliseconds with yesterday's data. Its latency SLO is doing fine. The person making a decision may be doing considerably worse.

For a useful freshness target, name the dataset, consumer, acceptable age, and owner. For example: a sales dataset available in a particular BI workflow within an agreed interval. The interval should come from the decision being supported, rather than whichever number looks impressive on the platform dashboard.

Measure the whole path: source delay, ingestion, validation, dataset readiness, BI refresh, and caches. Otherwise a fast ingestion service can conceal a slow extract schedule.

Freshness needs correctness beside it

Making the wrong number arrive sooner is not an improvement.

During migration, two recent datasets can disagree because they come from different paths. Before tightening the time bound, establish which path is authoritative, who owns critical fields, and how consumers learn about changes.

Check completeness as well as age. A dataset can have a recent timestamp and still be missing the records that matter.

Start with a promise you can keep

On the EDP migration, the practical commitments included migration support, acceptable query performance, deprecation dates, and a finite period of running both paths. Those commitments changed behaviour. A polished SLO document on its own would not have done that.

I would not describe every migration milestone as an SLO. A measured reliability target and a delivery commitment are different things. Both need owners, but only the former tells you how often an ongoing service promise is being met.

Start with one important consumer journey. Agree on the bound, measure breaches, and decide what changes when you miss it. If repeated misses never affect priorities, the target is decorative.

Product teams experience the number they can use. Measure that, even when the slowest part belongs to someone else.

entry.title: Saying no as a platform EM without becoming the villain
entry.summary:
A platform team can say yes to every request and still disappoint everyone. The work gets queued, exceptions accumulate, and the same engineers become responsible for more than they can operate.

As a platform EM, I found the useful part of saying no was making the alternative concrete: what we …
entry.content:
A platform team can say yes to every request and still disappoint everyone. The work gets queued, exceptions accumulate, and the same engineers become responsible for more than they can operate.

As a platform EM, I found the useful part of saying no was making the alternative concrete: what we could support, what it would cost, and who could change the priority.

Two situations from LinkedIn's Enterprise Data Platform (EDP) illustrate that.

No to an unfunded migration

BI teams using Power BI and Tableau already had Hadoop-based data paths. Asking them to adopt EDP because it was strategic did not give them time to migrate or reduce the risk to their dashboards.

The useful decision was to fund the transition. EDP engineers helped with connectors, migration, and performance. Leadership made deprecation a priority, with dates for ending the old paths.

That was more expensive than issuing a mandate. It also addressed the actual objection.

A platform cannot become the source of truth while treating the work of moving consumers onto it as somebody else's problem.

No to an indefinite architecture argument

On the self-serve portal, disagreement over monoliths and microservices held up execution for about a month. There were credible technical concerns on both sides, but no effective path to a decision.

We wrote evaluation criteria, time-boxed proofs of the alternatives, and brought in a neutral senior engineer. I also worked with the engineers on ownership and how they challenged each other.

The decision was hybrid: keep tightly integrated capabilities close to EDP, separate workflows where independent iteration helped, and centralise metadata with DataHub.

The point was not to find a compromise halfway between two preferences. It was to evaluate different needs separately and get the project moving again.

Put a price on exceptions

Temporary branches and dual pipelines may be necessary. Give each an owner, expiry, support cost, and removal condition.

An exception without those things is a permanent commitment nobody has budgeted for.

When declining new work, show the existing commitments and what would move if the request became a priority. Give partners an escalation path. “The team is busy” explains very little; a visible trade-off gives them something to decide.

A yes with no capacity is not kinder than a no. It just delays the disagreement until there is less time to resolve it.

entry.title: Identity systems fail socially before they fail cryptographically
entry.summary:
An identity system can validate every token correctly and still leave the wrong person with access.

The protocol matters. So do the decisions around it: who counts as the same person, who can grant access, what logout means, and who removes privileges when someone's role changes.

My work on identity …
entry.content:
An identity system can validate every token correctly and still leave the wrong person with access.

The protocol matters. So do the decisions around it: who counts as the same person, who can grant access, what logout means, and who removes privileges when someone's role changes.

My work on identity infrastructure made me wary of designs that spend all their attention on tokens and leave those workflows implicit.

Start with the person, not the token

Enterprise identities come from HR systems, directories, partner identity providers, and application databases. Those records will not always agree.

Define the subject identifier and who can change it. Account linking, splitting, and recovery need explicit procedures. Otherwise reconciliation scripts gradually become the place where your identity model actually lives.

SSO gives applications a common authentication path. It does not repair an ambiguous account model.

Temporary access needs an end

Demo accounts, support impersonation, integration users, and emergency access all have legitimate uses. They also create paths around normal controls.

Give exceptions an owner, expiry, and audit trail. Make removal a normal operation. A temporary bypass with no removal mechanism is simply a permanent bypass with optimistic documentation.

Break-glass access should remain usable during an incident. Its use should also be visible and reviewed afterwards.

Specify what logout and revocation mean

A user may end one application session while an identity-provider session or another application's refresh token remains valid. Whether that is a bug depends on the promised behaviour.

Define that behaviour across applications and devices. Distinguish local logout, global logout, token expiry, and access revocation. Test shared-device and account-recovery scenarios, not just a successful login.

For revocation, include downstream caches and propagation delay. Saying access was removed is incomplete if another service can still honour it for an hour.

Treat the login path as production infrastructure

Auth changes can prevent users from reaching everything else. Use progressive rollout, synthetic journeys, and rollback procedures that have been exercised.

Assign an operational owner for the end-to-end path. Security policy, identity-provider availability, application sessions, DNS, and recovery email may involve different teams. The incident still needs someone responsible for coordinating the response.

I would review cryptography and organisational workflows together. Neither compensates for the other. Correct token validation is little comfort when the entitlement was granted to the wrong account.

entry.title: What “led the web launch” taught me about constraints
entry.summary:
Putting Postman on the web meant moving a familiar desktop workflow into an environment with different rules.

Users expected collections, environments, and request execution to behave like Postman. Browsers restricted what we could do. Security, infrastructure, product scope, and a conference deadline all affected the design.

As the engineering manager …
entry.content:
Putting Postman on the web meant moving a familiar desktop workflow into an environment with different rules.

Users expected collections, environments, and request execution to behave like Postman. Browsers restricted what we could do. Security, infrastructure, product scope, and a conference deadline all affected the design.

As the engineering manager responsible for coordinating delivery, I spent as much time resolving those dependencies as discussing the implementation.

Familiar behaviour was a requirement

Developers already knew the desktop product. They would compare the web version with that experience, rather than treat missing capabilities as charming evidence of a new product.

We had to decide what to reuse, what to isolate, and which gaps to make explicit. Core workflow parity mattered more than having a clean rewrite.

The existing product carried knowledge about how users worked. Ignoring it would have meant learning the same lessons again, publicly.

Execution could not stay implicit

The desktop app could make network requests that a browser could not. CORS and access to private networks affected the basic Send workflow.

The product needed distinct execution paths:

  • A browser path for requests the browser could make.
  • A cloud path for supported requests executed outside the browser.
  • A desktop agent to reach local or private-network resources from the web UI.

Those paths had different reachability and security constraints. A cloud agent did not make every private target accessible, and a desktop bridge introduced its own dependency.

The architecture had to make those differences understandable without turning every request into a lesson on browser security.

Scope and rollout belonged together

We hit the conference launch window by phasing capability. The announcement did not mean every execution path and feature was equally mature.

A launch plan needs a working journey, explicit limits, a rollout sequence, and owners for the work afterwards. The first public version is when real traffic starts teaching you things the demo did not.

Cross-functional coordination was part of that plan. Dedicated capacity, regular unblock discussions, and written scope decisions helped prevent dependencies from drifting between teams.

Real workspaces reveal different problems

Large collections and histories made performance a product requirement. Efficient state handling, lazy loading, and virtualised lists mattered because developers brought existing work into the browser.

A small demo workspace is a poor benchmark for an established developer tool.

I would repeat the emphasis on explicit non-goals, journey-level instrumentation, partial-failure rehearsals, and capacity after launch. I would avoid betting a public date on a rewrite that was nearly ready.

The main lesson was to name the constraints early. The execution model and phased rollout followed from them. Drawing the web UI was the comparatively easy part.

entry.title: Incubating 0→1 beside a mature product
entry.summary:
A mature product gives you users, distribution, and a backlog large enough to bury most experiments.

At Postman, we wanted to explore protocols and workflows beyond the established HTTP client without taking capacity away from the product people already depended on. Postman Labs gave that work a separate place to …
entry.content:
A mature product gives you users, distribution, and a backlog large enough to bury most experiments.

At Postman, we wanted to explore protocols and workflows beyond the established HTTP client without taking capacity away from the product people already depended on. Postman Labs gave that work a separate place to develop.

The separation mattered. So did having a route back into the main product.

Protect exploration without disconnecting it

Labs used a small team familiar with Postman, lighter processes for experiments, and a clear success measure for each initiative.

The charter covered both new protocols and deeper workflows such as testing and automation. It gave the team permission to investigate without making every prototype a core-roadmap commitment.

That permission should include stopping. Otherwise you have created a feature team whose unfinished work is unusually difficult to question.

Make each phase earn the next

The sequence was feasibility and market validation, then an MVP used internally, then a limited beta.

Each phase answered a different question. Is there a problem worth solving? Can we build a usable solution? Does it remain useful to people outside the team?

A prototype proves that something can be demonstrated. It does not prove demand, supportability, or a reason to graduate it.

Dogfooding helped expose usability and correctness issues before public rollout. Developer-tool teams have a convenient supply of demanding users sitting nearby. It is sensible to use them.

New protocols change the workflow

WebSockets required persistent connections, bidirectional traffic, and an event history. Treating them as ordinary HTTP requests would have missed the reason developers wanted the capability.

gRPC brought Protobuf contracts, binary serialization, and unary and streaming calls. Users needed to compose requests and inspect what happened without leaving the tool.

Both required changes to the interaction model as well as network support. Their eventual place in Postman's broader product was the useful outcome of incubation.

Plan the graduation

A successful experiment needs owners for maintenance, reliability, documentation, and support. Core teams should be involved before that transfer becomes urgent.

Reserve exploration capacity, define a success measure, and write the graduation criteria. Review retained use rather than counting launches alone.

Too much process can kill an experiment early. Too little accountability can keep it alive forever. Labs needs room to discover something useful and enough discipline to recognise when it has not.

entry.title: How I review a distributed design in 45 minutes
entry.summary:
A design review can end with everyone understanding the diagram and nobody knowing what to do next.

On an EDP self-serve portal, disagreement over monoliths and microservices held up delivery for about a month. Both approaches had reasonable arguments. The discussion also undermined ownership, and the project stopped moving.

A …
entry.content:
A design review can end with everyone understanding the diagram and nobody knowing what to do next.

On an EDP self-serve portal, disagreement over monoliths and microservices held up delivery for about a month. Both approaches had reasonable arguments. The discussion also undermined ownership, and the project stopped moving.

A short review will not finish a distributed design. It can expose the assumptions and decisions that need more work. This is the structure I use when I have about forty-five minutes.

First, establish the promise

Spend the first five minutes on the user journey, scope, and non-goals.

For the portal, the job was dataset registration, access, governance, and metadata management. It was not an opportunity to rebuild the entire platform. That distinction removed quite a lot of architecture from the conversation.

Ask someone to walk through one real action. A sequence through the system tells me more than another diagram of service boxes.

Find the state that must be correct

For the next ten minutes, identify the system of record and the invariants.

Which operation must be atomic? What can be delayed? Where does metadata live? If two services disagree, which one wins, and how does the other recover?

For the portal, core capabilities depended closely on the existing EDP backend. Other workflows needed more independent iteration. Metadata lifecycle belonged in a shared catalog; we used DataHub.

Those were different needs. There was no reason they all had to get the same deployment model.

Walk through failure

Use another ten minutes for timeouts, retries, partial writes, replay, and dependency failure. Identify how the user sees a partial success and how an operator repairs it.

Also check ownership. Who can decide? Who runs the service? Who owns a failed interaction between teams? A technically sound design can still sit untouched if those answers are missing.

Decide what needs evidence

We used written criteria covering scalability, maintainability, delivery speed, and ownership. Both approaches got time-boxed proofs, with a neutral senior engineer helping evaluate them.

A proof should test the disputed assumption. It should not become a smaller implementation of each person's preferred architecture.

In parallel, I worked with the engineers on how disagreement was being handled. Restoring ownership was necessary for the technical decision to stick.

Leave with a decision and its limits

The result was a hybrid: keep tightly integrated core capabilities close to EDP, allow separate services where independent iteration justified them, and centralise metadata.

Write down the decision, owner, conditions, and what would cause a review. Reserve the final minutes for that record.

Forty-five minutes is a triage window, not an approval guarantee. If a critical invariant or recovery path remains unclear, the useful outcome is a named investigation. Approving a design just to finish the meeting is an expensive way to save five minutes.

entry.content:
Before we introduced a formal rotation at Postman, production issues were handled by whoever noticed and stepped in. Public GitHub reports added another route for problems to reach the team.

That arrangement looked flexible. In practice, ownership was unclear and the same people kept getting interrupted.

We needed predictable incident response without making reliability depend on a few engineers being permanently available.

Assign the work, then make room for it

We used primary and secondary roles.

The primary handled monitoring, incident response, and triage. Feature expectations dropped during that period. The secondary provided backup for major incidents, rather than becoming another primary for every message.

This capacity decision is easy to skip. If an engineer has the same delivery commitments plus operational responsibility, the schedule has not become more efficient. It has become fictional.

Our rotation used two-week windows, with a primary-to-secondary pattern to carry context forward. That cadence was a choice for our team, not a universal recommendation. Team size, incident frequency, and the demands outside working hours should determine the schedule.

Make the handoff useful

Weekly team time included incidents, resolutions, support themes, adjacent risks, and follow-ups. The outgoing primary explained what the next person needed to know.

Major incidents got retrospectives. Recurring problems got playbooks so the next engineer did not have to rediscover the same recovery steps.

A handoff should transfer unresolved work to an owner. It should not transfer a pile of links and hope.

Measure the burden as well as the service

The rotation made triage more systematic and spread production knowledge across the team. I would not attribute a precise response-time improvement to the rotation without a comparable baseline and incident mix.

For a new rotation, measure response time, alert volume, repeat incidents, after-hours interruptions, and how the work is distributed. Faster response is useful. Faster response achieved by repeatedly waking the same two people is not a sustainable result.

Noisy alerts need fixing. Repeated incidents need engineering time. Neither becomes acceptable because there is now a name on the rota.

Protect it after the launch

Avoid consecutive primary stretches where possible. Do not let the secondary become free extra capacity. Give retrospective actions owners and time to complete them.

The manager's job includes defending that capacity when feature deadlines arrive. Otherwise the old volunteer system returns, wearing a new calendar.

On-call made responsibility clearer for us. Keeping it useful required treating operational load as real work, every planning cycle.

entry.content:
When two revenue dashboards disagree, nobody is comforted by the fact that both pipelines succeeded.

The missing agreement is usually fairly basic: what does this number mean, who owns it, and which dataset should we trust?

Working on LinkedIn's Enterprise Data Platform (EDP) made those questions difficult to avoid. The platform was supposed to become the governed path for go-to-market data, while BI teams still had working Hadoop-based feeds. Adding another source did not automatically settle which one was right.

Agree on meaning before exposing the table

A data contract should explain what consumers are allowed to depend on. It needs more than field names and types.

For an important dataset, I want to know:

  • What one row represents, and which keys identify it.
  • What critical fields mean, including allowed nulls.
  • Who produces it and who uses it in production.
  • When it should be ready, and how complete it should be.
  • Who can change it, with what notice.
  • Which path is authoritative during migration.
  • Who responds when the agreement breaks.

This can fit in a short document. Length is not enforcement.

A field that retains its type but changes its meaning can break a dashboard more quietly than a schema change. Contracts need to cover semantics as well as syntax.

Make the agreement affect delivery

On EDP, connectors, migration support, and deprecation dates mattered because they made the governed path practical for BI consumers. A contract hidden in a wiki would not have moved their workbooks.

Validate the consumer path before cutover. Compare critical values during dual running. Check row counts and null rates, while recognising that those checks will not catch every semantic error. Give someone authority to stop a bad publish.

Producers own the meaning and correctness of their data. The platform provides discovery, access, and checks. BI partners own how the dataset is interpreted in their workflows. Shared responsibility still needs named people at each boundary.

Match the contract to the consequence

A temporary exploratory extract does not need the same process as a revenue metric used in leadership reviews. It does need an expiry if it is supposed to be temporary.

Start with the decision the dataset supports and the first production consumer. Write their expectations before widening access. End the old path when migration is complete.

Tables are easy to publish. A number that people can agree on takes more work.

entry.title: RDBMS vs. NOSQL?
entry.summary:
I came across Werner Vogels' article on DynamoDB while researching the database. His argument was that applications without a need for joins, complex queries, or transactions could be better served by a NoSQL store.

I respect Werner. I would still take that advice with a pinch of salt. Amazon also …
entry.content:
I came across Werner Vogels' article on DynamoDB while researching the database. His argument was that applications without a need for joins, complex queries, or transactions could be better served by a NoSQL store.

I respect Werner. I would still take that advice with a pinch of salt. Amazon also has a database to sell.

Most applications never reach the scale at which a relational database becomes their main problem. They do need a schema, queries, backups, monitoring, and people who know how to operate the system. Relational databases have a fairly good head start on all of those.

My starting point is a relational database unless a requirement makes that a poor fit. These are the requirements I would examine.

Availability beyond one server

A single database process is a point of failure. A crash or maintenance event can make the application unavailable.

If the availability target cannot tolerate that, evaluate replication, failover, or a distributed setup. That may be relational or non-relational. Choosing NoSQL does not by itself establish an availability guarantee.

Be explicit about the consistency you need during failures. “Always available” is not a useful requirement until you explain what answers the application is allowed to return.

Data that does not fit the model

Schemas help you express relationships and constraints. They also allow queries you did not anticipate on day one.

Some data does not fit that model neatly. Highly varied documents can justify a different store. Relational systems can accommodate some of this with features such as PostgreSQL's hstore and JSON support, but that does not mean every shape becomes pleasant to query.

Ask whether schema flexibility is a real need or simply a wish to avoid deciding what the data means. A database without a fixed schema does not remove that question from the application.

Growth beyond one machine

There is a limit to how much CPU, memory, and storage you can put on one server. If the expected workload exceeds it, you need a scaling plan.

That could involve partitioning, a relational cluster, or a non-relational store designed around the access pattern. Each choice adds operational and correctness work. Compare that cost with the workload you actually expect.

Most of the time, I would start with the system the team knows and can recover. Change it when a concrete requirement earns the extra complexity.

NoSQL is useful. So are relational databases. Neither needs you to join a side.
